title.en: Ramayana — Kishkindha Kanda (English Wiki Simple Full)

lessons.title: Lesson 01 — Hanuman meets Rama and Lakshmana
lessons.content: After Sita is abducted, Rama and Lakshmana wander the forests searching for her. They reach the region of Rishyamukha mountain, near the vanara (monkey) kingdom of Kishkindha. Sugriva, the exiled monkey prince, sees these two radiant warriors from a distance and becomes afraid that his brother Vali might have sent them to kill him. On Sugriva’s request, his wise minister Hanuman approaches Rama and Lakshmana in disguise as a brahmin ascetic. When he speaks with them, Hanuman quickly understands that Rama is the noble prince of Ayodhya and feels deep devotion arise in his heart. He reveals his true form, falls at Rama’s feet and offers help. Hanuman then takes Rama and Lakshmana to meet Sugriva on the mountain, where the prince explains how he was driven away by his brother Vali and is living in fear, waiting for divine help to arrive.

lessons.title: Lesson 02 — Rama’s friendship with Sugriva
lessons.content: On Rishyamukha, Sugriva welcomes Rama and Lakshmana and they share their stories. Sugriva tells how he once ruled Kishkindha while his elder brother Vali fought the demon Mayavi in a cave. When blood flowed out and Vali did not return for a long time, Sugriva thought his brother had died, closed the cave and took care of the kingdom to prevent chaos. But Vali eventually emerged alive, saw Sugriva on the throne and suspected betrayal. In anger he drove Sugriva out, seized his wife Ruma and threatened to kill him if he ever returned. Since Vali is protected by a boon that halves the strength of anyone who faces him, Sugriva has no way to fight back and hides on Rishyamukha, where Vali cannot enter. Hearing this, Rama feels compassion and promises to kill Vali and restore Sugriva’s honor in return for Sugriva’s help in finding Sita.

lessons.title: Lesson 03 — Sugriva’s doubts and Rama’s proof of strength
lessons.content: Sugriva sincerely wants to trust Rama, but he has seen Vali’s incredible strength and fears that even Rama might fail. To test Rama’s power, Sugriva shows him mighty signs of Vali’s feats, such as a huge saal tree that Vali pierced with a single arrow. Rama calmly listens to these stories and then demonstrates his own divine strength. With one arrow he pierces not just one tree, but a whole row of trees and even cracks a great rock beyond them. Sugriva is amazed and gains confidence that Rama can defeat Vali despite the boon. Encouraged, he agrees to challenge Vali to a duel, while Rama plans to stand aside and strike Vali at the right moment. This lesson shows how doubt is removed by direct experience, and how trust is formed between Rama and Sugriva before the decisive battle.

lessons.title: Lesson 04 — The fall of Vali
lessons.content: Following Rama’s advice, Sugriva goes to the city of Kishkindha and loudly calls Vali to combat. Tara, Vali’s wise queen, senses danger and warns him that Sugriva would not dare return unless a powerful ally is supporting him. But Vali’s pride blinds him, and he rushes out to fight. In their first encounter Rama does not shoot, because the brothers look alike and he cannot clearly distinguish them. Sugriva is badly beaten and runs back, upset that Rama did not help. Rama explains the problem and asks him to wear a flower garland as a clear mark. Sugriva again challenges Vali. A fierce duel begins, shaking the earth. This time, as the garlanded Sugriva struggles, Rama releases a deadly arrow from hiding. It strikes Vali in the chest and he falls mortally wounded. The mighty king of Kishkindha, who once terrorized his enemies, lies defeated through Rama’s hidden arrow.

lessons.title: Lesson 05 — Vali’s questions and Rama’s sorrow
lessons.content: As Vali lies on the battlefield, he questions Rama: why did a righteous prince kill him from concealment instead of facing him directly? Vali argues that Rama could have simply asked for help in the search for Sita, and he would have gladly fought Ravana. Rama gently explains that as a king of Ayodhya, he must uphold dharma everywhere. Vali had committed serious wrongs by taking his brother’s wife and unjustly seizing his kingdom. By supporting the weaker, innocent party and punishing the oppressor, Rama says he is acting as a guardian of righteousness, not as a personal enemy. Hearing this, Vali’s pride softens. He recognizes Rama’s divinity, seeks forgiveness and instructs his son Angada to serve Sugriva and assist Rama. Rama still feels the weight of taking a life and remembers his separation from Sita, but he accepts this act as part of his duty to protect dharma.

lessons.title: Lesson 06 — Lakshmana’s anger at Sugriva
lessons.content: After Vali’s death, Rama installs Sugriva as king of Kishkindha and makes Angada the crown prince. Sugriva regains his wife Ruma and the kingdom begins to enjoy peace. Rama and Lakshmana move to the nearby Prasravana mountain and wait for the rainy season to pass before starting the search for Sita. As the months go by, Sugriva becomes absorbed in royal pleasures and forgets his promise. The rains end, but the search does not begin. Rama quietly endures, but Lakshmana is deeply upset that Sugriva has neglected his sacred vow. At Rama’s request, Lakshmana goes to Kishkindha to remind him. Burning with anger, he storms through the gates and threatens to destroy the city. The monkeys tremble with fear. Tara wisely comes forward, calms Lakshmana and gently leads Sugriva back to his senses. Sugriva sincerely repents, asks forgiveness from Rama and orders preparations for a great search.

lessons.title: Lesson 07 — The great search for Sita begins
lessons.content: Awakened by Tara’s counsel and Lakshmana’s warning, Sugriva now fulfills his duty. He gathers vast armies of vanaras and bears from every region. Rama explains that Sita may be held anywhere on earth or across the seas, so the search must cover all directions. Sugriva divides the warriors into separate groups and assigns experienced leaders to each: some are sent to the north, some to the east, some to the west, and one powerful group to the south. Rama trusts above all in Hanuman’s devotion and capacity, so he especially relies on the southern party, which includes Hanuman, Angada, Jambavan and many other heroes. Before they depart, Rama gives Hanuman his signet ring as a sacred token for Sita, asking him to comfort her and convey his unbroken love. With blessings from Rama and Sugriva, the search for Sita finally begins in earnest.

lessons.title: Lesson 08 — The southern search and Sampati’s revelation
lessons.content: Hanuman, Angada, Jambavan and their companions travel south through forests, mountains and deserts, tirelessly asking about Sita but finding no clear trace. Exhausted and thirsty, they reach a seashore and despair that their efforts have failed. At this moment they notice a strange, wingless vulture named Sampati, living in a cave by the shore. He reveals that he is the elder brother of Jatayu, the noble bird who died trying to rescue Sita from Ravana. Hearing Jatayu’s name, Sampati is moved and tells his own story: how he once saved Jatayu from the scorching sun, lost his wings and fell to earth. From his high vantage point over the years, he has seen distant lands across the ocean. Sampati then tells the vanaras that Sita is held captive in the golden city of Lanka, far across the sea, and urges them to find a way to reach it.

lessons.title: Lesson 09 — Jambavan reminds Hanuman of his power
lessons.content: After learning from Sampati that Sita is in Lanka, the vanaras face a new challenge: someone must cross the vast ocean in a single mighty leap. Each hero estimates his own strength. Some can jump a great distance but not return; others fall short of the required span. As they discuss, Hanuman sits quietly, modest and withdrawn, forgetting his own greatness because of a curse that once made him unaware of his powers. The wise elder Jambavan then speaks, reminding Hanuman of his divine birth, his childhood feats and the blessings he received from powerful gods. He explains that Hanuman was truly born to serve Rama and accomplish this very task. Inspired by Jambavan’s words, Hanuman’s confidence awakens. He grows in size and radiance, roars Rama’s name and resolves to leap to Lanka in a single bound. With this, Kishkindha Kanda ends and the glorious Sundara Kanda begins.
